subject: SE = 0 and Z= NA  with  standardizedSolution(), why?

messages.author: 809c86ffe9d447f3
messages.subject: SE = 0 and Z= NA  with  standardizedSolution(), why?
parts:
Hi Everyone, 

I am trying to understand why I am getting the following result:

When I extract my path model results with standardizedSolution() (It was highlighted in another thread that this is what I should do if I scale my data before fitting my models) some of my (self-defined) indirect effects have SE's equal to zero and thus the Z-values and P-values are set to NA. 

This is not the case when I use parameterEstimates() to examine my results. 

Can someone tell my why this might be happening and what can I do if I am seeking to report z-values and p-values?

Many many thanks!

Sofia

messages.author: bc810b1d0900407f
messages.subject: Re: SE = 0 and Z= NA with standardizedSolution(), why?
parts:
Dear Sofia,

I read your post in the other thread. I did not reply, yet, because I am still trying to understand that case you mentioned.

May you share an example to illustrate the problem you found?

I am not sure whether this is always the case but se = 0 and z = NA in the output usually mean that the parameter is fixed or constrained to a particular value (it can be constrained to a sample value, e.g., the variance of a variable treated as fixed). This also happens to correlations in standardizedSolution().

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject: Re: SE = 0 and Z= NA with standardizedSolution(), why?
parts: > This also happens to correlations in standardizedSolution().

I meant this also happens to the *variances* of some variables in standardizedSolution(), e.g., variances of latent factors in a CFA model are constrained to one (so se = 0 and z = NA) because this is needed to get the correlations between latent factors.

-- Shu Fai

Hi Shu Fai, 

Thank you for replying to this - I had to take some time to figure out how to properly come back to this question. 

In my model I am not really working with fixed parameters or latent variables. I am really just running a Path model. 

I have figured out that the cases in which I get SE=0 and Z=NA are for certain indirect effects/paths only, and what seems to make these effects special is that they are incredibly small. For instance, the coefficient for some path a*b*c = -0.000008. Paths like these are the ones that tend to have SE = 0. 

Could it be the case that by having such a small coefficient the variance is taken to be zero? and thus SE =0. 

Best,
Sofia
